opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually very human, and I don't see it as a character flaw. When you've spent ten or twenty years building expertise in a particular way of doing things, a new method isn't just a technical choice. It threatens the value of everything you've invested in. If deep learning works, a lot of your hand-engineered features, your carefully tuned pipelines, your intuitions about what matters, suddenly look less important. That's a hard thing to accept emotionally, even if you're a very rational person.

There's also a legitimate side to it. Established researchers have seen a lot of hype cycles come and go. They've watched methods that looked amazing on one benchmark completely fall apart in the real world. So some skepticism is earned. They're asking, "Is this real, or is this another fad?" And honestly, that's a healthy question for a field to ask.

What I've noticed is that the turning point usually isn't an argument. It's the tooling. People don't switch because you convinced them in a debate. They switch when the new thing becomes easy enough to try that they can see it work on their own problem in an afternoon. That's a big part of why I care so much about building tools. When the cost of experimenting goes down, the reluctance kind of melts away, because people no longer have to bet their careers on something to find out whether it works. They can just try it.

So I try to be empathetic about it. The goal isn't to win the argument with the senior folks. It's to lower the barrier enough that curiosity wins over caution.

r001.rationale: The candidate says years spent building expertise make a new method feel like a threat to the value of that investment.

r002.rationale: The candidate says experienced researchers have seen hype cycles and methods fail outside benchmarks, prompting them to ask whether a new method is real or another fad.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that research is a social thing, not just an intellectual thing. When you've spent ten or fifteen years building intuition in one paradigm, your whole mental toolkit is calibrated to it. You know what a good result looks like, you know what the failure modes are, you know which ideas are worth chasing. A new method doesn't just ask you to learn something, it asks you to throw away a lot of that calibration and go back to being a beginner, and that's genuinely uncomfortable.

I saw this very directly with deep learning around 2012, 2013. There were a lot of people in computer vision who had very principled, very well-understood approaches, and then suddenly these neural networks come along that work better but you can't really explain why. For someone who cares a lot about understanding, that feels like a step backwards, even if the numbers are better. So I don't think the reluctance is irrational. It's partly a different value system about what counts as progress.

And then there's the incentive side. If you're established, you have students, you have grants, you have a reputation tied to a certain line of work. Switching is costly, and the payoff is uncertain. Whereas if you're a grad student with nothing to lose, you'll happily try the weird new thing because the downside is small.

What I try to remember is that skepticism is also useful. Not every new method survives, and the people pushing back are often asking the questions that make the method better. The problem is only when skepticism turns into dismissal, when people stop engaging with the evidence. I think the healthiest thing a field can do is make it cheap to try new things, so the argument gets settled by experiments rather than by status. That was honestly a big part of why we cared so much about making tools like PyTorch easy to use. If it takes a week to try an idea instead of six months, people's priors matter a lot less.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers who have spent ten or fifteen years building expertise and intuition may resist giving up that calibration to become beginners again.

r002.rationale: It says not every new method survives, but does not connect experienced researchers’ exposure to past scientific fads with their skepticism about a new method’s staying power.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very human. When you’ve spent twenty or thirty years developing an approach, you’ve built both expertise and an intuition for what good work looks like. A new method can challenge that intuition, and suddenly a lot of what made you successful may not seem as valuable. So there’s an intellectual question—does this actually work?—but there’s also an emotional cost to taking it seriously.

And skepticism is useful. You don’t want everyone abandoning established methods every time something new shows promise. The distinction, to me, is whether you’re willing to update when the evidence becomes convincing. You can have a high bar for evidence and still be open to being surprised.

r001.rationale: It says researchers have spent decades building expertise and intuition, and that a new method can make the value of that investment feel threatened.

r002.rationale: It describes useful skepticism and the need for convincing evidence, but does not connect skepticism to prior scientific fads or concern that a new method will not endure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very human. If you’ve spent twenty years developing an intuition for a particular way of doing science, a new method isn’t just another tool. It can challenge your judgment about what good work looks like, and even the value of what you’ve spent your career doing.

And some skepticism is healthy. A new method might produce impressive results without giving us a clear understanding of why it works or when it fails. You should ask those questions. The problem is when “I don’t understand this yet” becomes “this isn’t a legitimate way to do science.”

Ideally, you stay skeptical while remaining willing to update. You ask what evidence would change your mind, and you give the new approach a fair chance to produce that evidence. That’s difficult for all of us, especially when our expertise and identity are tied together.

r001.rationale: The response says that after spending twenty years developing an approach, a new method can challenge researchers’ judgment and the value of their career’s work.

r002.rationale: It describes skepticism about understanding why a method works or when it fails, but does not connect skepticism to past scientific fads or whether a new method will endure.
